description: Master relational databases, SQL queries, constraints, and data modeling to manage and retrieve data efficiently.

topics.title: What is a Database?
topics.content:
Tutorials > Web Development > SQL > Basics

What is a Database?

Beginner ⏱️ 5 min read

A database is an organized collection of structured information, or data, typically stored electronically in a computer system. A database is usually controlled by a database management system (DBMS).

Key Concepts

  • Data: Facts and statistics collected together for reference or analysis.
  • Table: A collection of related data held in a structured format within a database. It consists of columns and rows.
  • Row (Record): A single, implicitly structured data item in a table.
  • Column (Field): A set of data values of a particular simple type, one value for each row of the database.

topics.title: Database Management Systems (DBMS)
topics.content:
Tutorials > Web Development > SQL > Basics

Database Management Systems (DBMS)

Beginner ⏱️ 6 min read

A Database Management System (DBMS) is software that interacts with end-users, applications, and the database itself to capture and analyze the data. The DBMS software additionally encompasses the core facilities provided to administer the database.

RDBMS (Relational DBMS)

An RDBMS is a type of DBMS that stores data in a row-based table structure which connects related data elements. RDBMS includes functions that maintain the security, accuracy, integrity, and consistency of the data. SQL is the standard language used to interact with an RDBMS.

Popular RDBMS Examples

  • MySQL
  • PostgreSQL
  • Oracle Database
  • Microsoft SQL Server
  • SQLite

topics.title: SQL Command Types (DDL, DML, DCL, TCL)
topics.content:
Tutorials > Web Development > SQL > Basics

Types of SQL Commands

Core Concept ⏱️ 8 min read

SQL commands are instructions used to communicate with the database. They are broadly categorized into four types:

1. DDL (Data Definition Language)

Used to define the database structure or schema.

  • CREATE: Creates a new table, database, schema, etc.
  • ALTER: Modifies an existing database object.
  • DROP: Deletes an entire table, view of a table, or other objects in the database.
  • TRUNCATE: Removes all records from a table, but not its structure.

2. DML (Data Manipulation Language)

Used for managing data within schema objects.

  • SELECT: Retrieves data from the database.
  • INSERT: Inserts data into a table.
  • UPDATE: Updates existing data within a table.
  • DELETE: Deletes records from a table.

3. DCL (Data Control Language)

Used to control access to data in the database.

  • GRANT: Gives user access privileges to database.
  • REVOKE: Withdraws user access privileges.

4. TCL (Transaction Control Language)

Used to manage transactions in the database.

  • COMMIT: Commits a transaction.
  • ROLLBACK: Rollbacks a transaction in case of any error occurs.
  • SAVEPOINT: Sets a savepoint within a transaction.

topics.title: Basic SQL Queries
topics.content:
Tutorials > Web Development > SQL > SQL

Basic SQL Queries

Essential ⏱️ 15 min read

SQL queries allow you to manage databases, create tables, and manipulate data (retrieve, insert, update, and delete).

Create and Drop Databases

Before doing anything with data, you must first create a database using CREATE DATABASE. To delete it, use DROP DATABASE.

Database Queries Syntax
CREATE DATABASE databasename;
DROP DATABASE databasename;

The CREATE TABLE Statement

The CREATE TABLE statement is used to create a new table in a database. You must specify the name of the table and the columns (along with their data types).

CREATE TABLE Syntax
CREATE TABLE Users (
    ID int,
    Name varchar(255),
    Age int
);

The SELECT Statement

The SELECT statement is used to select data from a database. The data returned is stored in a result table, called the result-set.

SELECT Syntax
SELECT column1, column2 FROM table_name;

The WHERE Clause

The WHERE clause is used to filter records. It is used to extract only those records that fulfill a specified condition.

WHERE Syntax
SELECT * FROM table_name WHERE condition;

INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE

These commands are used to modify data in the tables.

-- Insert a new record
INSERT INTO Users (Name, Age) VALUES ('Alice', 30);

-- Update an existing record
UPDATE Users SET Age = 31 WHERE Name = 'Alice';

-- Delete a record
DELETE FROM Users WHERE Name = 'Alice';

topics.title: SQL Constraints
topics.content:
Tutorials > Web Development > SQL > SQL

SQL Constraints

Core Concept ⏱️ 10 min read

What are Constraints?

Constraints are rules applied to table columns to ensure the accuracy, consistency, and integrity of the data stored in a database. In simple words, constraints prevent invalid data from being inserted into the database.

Why do we use Constraints?

Imagine a student database. Every student should have a unique ID, student name should not be empty, email should not be duplicated, admission date should have today's date if not provided, and student ID should automatically increase. All these rules are implemented using constraints.

Types of Constraints

1. PRIMARY KEY

A PRIMARY KEY is a column (or combination of columns) that uniquely identifies each row in a table. Values must be unique, cannot contain NULL, and only one PRIMARY KEY is allowed per table.

PRIMARY KEY Example
CREATE TABLE Student(
    student_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    student_name VARCHAR(100)
);

2. NOT NULL

The NOT NULL constraint ensures that a column must always contain a value. It prevents empty values.

NOT NULL Example
CREATE TABLE Employee(
    id INT,
    name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL
);

3. UNIQUE

The UNIQUE constraint ensures that all values in a column are different. Duplicate values are not allowed. Unlike PRIMARY KEY, a table can have multiple UNIQUE constraints (e.g., Email, Aadhaar Number, Passport Number).

PRIMARY KEY UNIQUE
Only one per table Many allowed
Cannot be NULL Can contain NULL
Uniquely identifies each row Ensures unique values
Automatically indexed Automatically indexed

4. DEFAULT

The DEFAULT constraint automatically assigns a value if the user does not provide one during insertion.

DEFAULT Example
CREATE TABLE Employee(
    id INT,
    salary DECIMAL(10,2) DEFAULT 15000
);

5. AUTO_INCREMENT

AUTO_INCREMENT automatically generates sequential numbers whenever a new record is inserted. No need to manually enter IDs.

AUTO_INCREMENT Example
CREATE TABLE Student(
    id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
    name VARCHAR(100)
);

INSERT INTO Student(name)
VALUES ('Mohamed'), ('Rahul'), ('Priya');

topics.title: Primary Key
topics.content:
Tutorials > Web Development > SQL > SQL

Primary Key

Essential ⏱️ 6 min read

The PRIMARY KEY constraint uniquely identifies each record in a table.

Characteristics of a Primary Key

  • Primary keys must contain UNIQUE values.
  • A primary key column cannot contain NULL values.
  • A table can have only ONE primary key.
  • The primary key can consist of single or multiple columns (composite key).
Creating a Primary Key
CREATE TABLE Persons (
    ID int NOT NULL,
    LastName varchar(255) NOT NULL,
    FirstName varchar(255),
    Age int,
    PRIMARY KEY (ID)
);

topics.title: Unique Key
topics.content:
Tutorials > Web Development > SQL > SQL

Unique Key

Essential ⏱️ 5 min read

The UNIQUE constraint ensures that all values in a column are different.

UNIQUE vs PRIMARY KEY

Both the UNIQUE and PRIMARY KEY constraints provide a guarantee for uniqueness for a column or set of columns.

A PRIMARY KEY constraint automatically has a UNIQUE constraint. However, you can have many UNIQUE constraints per table, but only one PRIMARY KEY constraint per table.

Creating a Unique Key
CREATE TABLE Persons (
    ID int NOT NULL,
    LastName varchar(255) NOT NULL,
    FirstName varchar(255),
    Age int,
    UNIQUE (ID)
);

topics.title: SQL Data Types
topics.content:
Tutorials > Web Development > SQL > SQL

SQL Data Types

Core Concept ⏱️ 15 min read

What is a Data Type?

A Data Type defines the type of value that can be stored in a table column. It tells MySQL what kind of data can be stored, how much storage space is required, and what operations can be performed on the data.

Example Table with Data Types
CREATE TABLE Student(
    id INT,
    name VARCHAR(100),
    age INT,
    fees DECIMAL(10,2),
    dob DATE
);

Categories of Data Types in MySQL

MySQL data types are divided into 5 categories:

1. Numeric Data Types

Used to store numbers. Divided into Integer Types and Decimal/Floating Point Types.

Data Type Storage Example Usage
TINYINT1 ByteAge
SMALLINT2 BytesMarks
MEDIUMINT3 BytesPopulation
INT4 BytesStudent ID
BIGINT8 BytesLarge IDs

Decimal Types:

  • FLOAT: Approximate decimal values. Used for height, weight, scientific calculations. May lose precision.
  • DOUBLE: More accurate than FLOAT. Suitable for GPS coordinates, large decimal calculations.
  • DECIMAL: Stores exact decimal values (e.g., DECIMAL(10,2) means 10 digits total, 2 after decimal).

2. String (Character) Data Types

Used to store text.

  • CHAR: Fixed-length string. Suitable for Gender, Country Code, Blood Group.
  • VARCHAR: Variable-length string. Suitable for Name, Address, Email.
  • TEXT: Stores very large text. Suitable for Feedback, Comments, Articles.

3. Date and Time Data Types

Used to store date and time.

Data Type Stores
DATEDate only
TIMETime only
DATETIMEDate + Time
TIMESTAMPDate + Time (often auto-managed)
YEARYear only

4. Boolean Data Type

MySQL treats BOOLEAN as an alias for TINYINT(1).

5. Binary Data Types

Used to store binary data such as images, files, or encrypted content.

  • BINARY: Fixed-length binary data.
  • VARBINARY: Variable-length binary data (e.g., password hash).
  • BLOB: Stores large binary data like images, PDFs, audio, video.

Complete Example

Comprehensive Table Creation
CREATE TABLE Employee(
    id INT PRIMARY KEY,
    name VARCHAR(100),
    age TINYINT,
    salary DECIMAL(10,2),
    email VARCHAR(100),
    gender CHAR(1),
    department ENUM('HR','IT','Sales'),
    skills SET('Java','Python','React','SQL'),
    joining_date DATE,
    login_time TIME,
    created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    isActive BOOLEAN,
    profile_photo BLOB
);

topics.title: Quiz

quiz.question: What is the fundamental functional difference between the 'WHERE' clause and the 'HAVING' clause in SQL?
options: No difference; they are completely interchangeable
'WHERE' filters individual rows before grouping or aggregation; 'HAVING' filters aggregated group records after the 'GROUP BY' clause has been processed
'HAVING' can only be used with subqueries
'WHERE' is only used for numerical values
quiz.explanation: 'WHERE' filters individual rows before aggregation functions are evaluated. 'HAVING' filters aggregated rows created by the 'GROUP BY' clause (e.g. HAVING COUNT(*) > 5).

quiz.question: Which JOIN type returns all records from the left table and matching records from the right table, populating NULL for non-matching right table columns?
options: INNER JOIN
LEFT JOIN (LEFT OUTER JOIN)
FULL OUTER JOIN
CROSS JOIN
quiz.explanation: A LEFT JOIN preserves every row from the left-hand table. If no corresponding match exists in the right-hand table, all right-hand column values in that row will be NULL.

quiz.question: What does the 'A' in ACID properties of relational database transactions guarantee?
options: Asynchronous execution
Atomicity: guarantees that all operations within a transaction complete successfully or the entire transaction is rolled back with zero changes applied (all-or-nothing)
Authentication
Association
quiz.explanation: Atomicity ensures that transactions are treated as single indivisible units of work: either all database statements succeed or, upon failure, the entire transaction is rolled back.

quiz.question: What is the key operational difference between 'TRUNCATE' and 'DELETE' statements in SQL?
options: DELETE cannot be rolled back; TRUNCATE can always be rolled back

DELETE is a DML command that removes rows one by one, writes row deletions to the transaction log, supports WHERE clauses, and fires triggers; TRUNCATE is a DDL command that deallocates entire data pages, is faster, and cannot have a WHERE clause
TRUNCATE deletes the table schema definition itself
There is no difference
quiz.explanation: DELETE (DML) logs row deletions individually and fires triggers, allowing row-level WHERE filtering. TRUNCATE (DDL) deallocates data pages directly, resets identity counters, and operates significantly faster.

quiz.question: What data structure is most universally utilized for relational database indexes to support fast lookups and range scans?
options: Binary Heap
B-Tree / B+Tree
Hash Table only
Linked List
quiz.explanation: B+Trees maintain sorted keys with balanced depth. Leaf nodes are linked sequentially, allowing both O(log n) random key lookups and highly efficient range-based scans.

quiz.question: What is the difference between 'UNION' and 'UNION ALL' when combining the results of two SELECT queries?
options: UNION ALL removes duplicate records; UNION keeps all duplicates
UNION performs a distinct sort operation to eliminate duplicate rows from the final result; UNION ALL combines all rows from both sets without removing duplicates, making it faster
UNION only works with numbers
UNION ALL requires identical table names
quiz.explanation: UNION deduplicates the combined dataset (incurring a sort/hash overhead). UNION ALL simply concatenates result sets without deduplication, offering superior query performance.

quiz.question: What is the difference between 'COUNT(*)' and 'COUNT(column_name)'?
options: No difference
'COUNT(*)' counts all rows in the group including rows with NULL values; 'COUNT(column_name)' counts only rows where the specified column is NOT NULL
'COUNT(*)' is slower than 'COUNT(column)'
'COUNT(column)' returns 0 if any row is null
quiz.explanation: COUNT(*) tallies all rows returned by the query regardless of contents. COUNT(column_name) evaluates and excludes NULL values from the total count.

quiz.question: Which SQL constraint ensures that all values in a column are unique and automatically prevents NULL values?
options: UNIQUE
PRIMARY KEY
FOREIGN KEY
CHECK
quiz.explanation: A PRIMARY KEY uniquely identifies each record in a table. It implicitly combines UNIQUE and NOT NULL constraints. Standard UNIQUE constraints typically allow one or more NULL values.

quiz.question: What does the 'ON DELETE CASCADE' clause on a Foreign Key constraint enforce?
quiz.code: CONSTRAINT fk_user FOREIGN KEY (user_id) REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE
options: Prevents the parent record from being deleted
Automatically deletes all associated child rows in this table whenever the corresponding referenced parent row is deleted
Sets the foreign key column to NULL upon parent deletion
Archives deleted rows into a backup table
quiz.explanation: 'ON DELETE CASCADE' automatically propagates parent row deletions to dependent child rows, preventing orphaned records and foreign key constraint violations.

quiz.question: What is the difference between 'RANK()' and 'DENSE_RANK()' window functions when ranking ties?
options: No difference
'RANK()' assigns identical ranks to ties but skips subsequent rank numbers (e.g. 1, 2, 2, 4); 'DENSE_RANK()' assigns identical ranks to ties without skipping subsequent numbers (e.g. 1, 2, 2, 3)
'DENSE_RANK()' only ranks descending order
'RANK()' returns floating point values
quiz.explanation: When ties occur: RANK() introduces gaps in the ranking sequence (1, 2, 2, 4). DENSE_RANK() leaves no gaps (1, 2, 2, 3). ROW_NUMBER() always assigns strict sequential integers (1, 2, 3, 4).

quiz.question: What does the 'COALESCE(val1, val2, val3)' function return?
quiz.code: SELECT COALESCE(phone, mobile, 'N/A') FROM contacts;
options: Concatenates all non-null values together
Returns the first non-null expression from the argument list, or NULL if all arguments evaluate to NULL
Counts the number of null values
Returns the maximum value
quiz.explanation: COALESCE() evaluates its arguments sequentially from left to right and returns the first non-NULL expression, providing a clean fallback mechanism.

quiz.question: In an SQL LIKE pattern, what do the '%' and '_' wildcard characters represent?
quiz.code: SELECT * FROM users WHERE name LIKE 'J_n%';
options: '%' matches exactly one character; '_' matches zero or more characters
'%' matches zero, one, or multiple characters; '_' matches exactly one single character
Both characters match any single digit
'%' matches numbers; '_' matches letters
quiz.explanation: In SQL LIKE clauses: '%' matches any sequence of zero or more characters. '_' matches exactly one single character (e.g. 'J_n%' matches 'Jane', 'Jonny', 'Junior').

quiz.question: What is a Correlated Subquery in SQL?
options: A subquery that runs once before the outer query starts
A subquery that references columns from the enclosing outer query and is evaluated once for each candidate row processed by the outer query
A subquery that joins two databases
A subquery containing a UNION
quiz.explanation: A correlated subquery references columns from the outer query. Because it depends on outer row data, it re-evaluates repeatedly for every row considered by the outer query.

quiz.question: What is the difference between 'EXISTS' and 'IN' when evaluating subqueries?
options: No difference
'EXISTS' tests for the existence of rows and short-circuits to TRUE as soon as a single match is located; 'IN' scans and evaluates the entire subquery result set and handles NULLs differently
'IN' is always faster than 'EXISTS'
'EXISTS' cannot be used with WHERE
quiz.explanation: EXISTS returns a boolean as soon as the first matching row is found (short-circuit). IN compiles an in-memory list and can yield unexpected results if NULL values are present (NOT IN with NULL returns empty).

quiz.question: What is Database Normalization and what is its primary objective?
options: To increase the speed of SELECT queries by duplicating data across tables
To organize database schemas to eliminate redundant data and prevent insertion, update, and deletion anomalies
To convert SQL tables into JSON files
To compress disk storage using gzip
quiz.explanation: Normalization organizes relational tables to ensure dependencies make sense (1NF, 2NF, 3NF), minimizing duplicate data to prevent data inconsistency and modification anomalies.

quiz.question: What requirement must a table satisfy to be in Third Normal Form (3NF)?
options: It must be in 2NF and have no partial key dependencies
It must be in 2NF and contain NO transitive dependencies (no non-key attribute can depend on another non-key attribute)
It must have no foreign keys
All columns must be strings
quiz.explanation: 3NF requires a relation to be in 2NF and have every non-prime attribute non-transitively dependent on the primary key (X -> Y requires X to be a super key or Y to be a prime attribute).

quiz.question: What is the difference between a Clustered Index and a Non-Clustered Index?
options: A table can have multiple clustered indexes but only one non-clustered index

A Clustered Index dictates the physical order in which actual table rows are stored on disk (only one per table, usually the Primary Key); a Non-Clustered Index stores sorted keys with pointers back to the data rows
Non-clustered indexes are stored in RAM only
Clustered indexes are slower for range scans
quiz.explanation: A clustered index physically sorts and stores data rows on disk (hence max 1 per table). Non-clustered indexes are separate auxiliary B-Trees containing indexed columns and row locators/pointers.

quiz.question: What is a Common Table Expression (CTE) in SQL?
options: A temporary physical table saved to disk
A named temporary result set defined within the execution scope of a single SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE statement using the 'WITH' clause
A database trigger
An encrypted view
quiz.explanation: A CTE (Common Table Expression) created with 'WITH name AS (...)' provides a readable, modular, and optionally recursive temporary query block that exists only during query execution.

quiz.question: What does a CROSS JOIN produce?
quiz.code: SELECT * FROM colors CROSS JOIN sizes;
options: Only matching rows between both tables
The Cartesian Product: every row from the first table paired with every row from the second table (M * N rows)
An empty table
A full outer join without nulls
quiz.explanation: A CROSS JOIN produces the Cartesian product of the two tables. If table A has 5 rows and table B has 10 rows, the result contains 50 rows.

quiz.question: What is a SELF JOIN?
options: A query that joins a table to itself using table aliases to represent parent-child or hierarchical relationships
A join between two databases on the same host
An automatic query without an ON clause
A circular dependency error
quiz.explanation: A self-join joins a table to itself using distinct aliases (e.g. employee 'e' and manager 'm'), commonly used to model hierarchies, organizational charts, or sequential events.

quiz.question: Which transaction isolation level provides the highest degree of isolation and completely prevents Dirty Reads, Non-Repeatable Reads, and Phantom Reads?
options: READ UNCOMMITTED
READ COMMITTED
REPEATABLE READ
SERIALIZABLE
quiz.explanation: SERIALIZABLE is the strictest ACID isolation level. It executes concurrent transactions as if they were processed sequentially one after another, eliminating dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and phantom reads.

quiz.question: What is a 'Dirty Read' in database transaction concurrency?
options: Reading corrupt disk sectors
A transaction reads uncommitted changes made by another concurrently running transaction that might subsequently be rolled back
Reading data without an index
Reading deleted foreign keys
quiz.explanation: A dirty read occurs when Transaction A reads data modified by Transaction B before Transaction B commits. If B rolls back, Transaction A operated on invalid, phantom data.

quiz.question: What is the difference between a 'Non-Repeatable Read' and a 'Phantom Read'?
options: No difference

Non-Repeatable Read occurs when re-reading the SAME row yields modified column data; Phantom Read occurs when re-executing a range query yields NEWLY INSERTED or deleted rows matching the search criteria
Phantom reads only happen in MySQL
Non-repeatable reads happen during database backup
quiz.explanation: Non-repeatable read: an existing row's values change between reads due to an UPDATE. Phantom read: the set of rows satisfying a query range predicate changes due to concurrent INSERT/DELETE.

quiz.question: What is the function of the 'EXPLAIN' or 'EXPLAIN ANALYZE' command in SQL?
quiz.code: EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 450;
options: Translates SQL to English sentences
Displays the Query Execution Plan generated by the database optimizer, detailing index scans, sequential scans, join algorithms, estimated costs, and actual runtime execution timings
Checks for SQL syntax errors without running
Repairs corrupted table indexes
quiz.explanation: EXPLAIN displays the database optimizer's planned execution steps (Index Scan vs Seq Scan, Hash Join vs Nested Loop, buffer usage, and execution timings), essential for query optimization.

quiz.question: What does the 'NULLIF(a, b)' function return?
quiz.code: SELECT 100 / NULLIF(divisor, 0) FROM calculations;
options: Returns a if a is null
Returns NULL if both arguments are equal (a == b); otherwise returns the first argument 'a'
Throws an error if either argument is null
Returns 0
quiz.explanation: NULLIF(a, b) returns NULL if a = b; otherwise it returns a. It is universally employed to prevent division-by-zero errors (NULLIF(divisor, 0) turns 0 into NULL, yielding NULL instead of crashing).

quiz.question: What happens when you compare a column to NULL using '= NULL' instead of 'IS NULL'?
quiz.code: SELECT * FROM users WHERE status = NULL;
options: Returns all rows where status is NULL
Returns an empty result set (0 rows) because in SQL, comparison with NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN (Three-Valued Logic), never TRUE
Throws a compile-time syntax error
Returns all non-null rows
quiz.explanation: In SQL's Three-Valued Logic (TRUE, FALSE, UNKNOWN), any equality comparison with NULL (e.g. col = NULL) yields UNKNOWN. Since WHERE requires TRUE, zero rows are returned. You must use 'IS NULL'.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of a Database View ('CREATE VIEW')?
quiz.code:
CREATE VIEW active_customers AS 
SELECT id, name, email FROM customers WHERE active = true;
options: Creates an identical physical copy of the table on disk
Creates a virtual table defined by an underlying stored SQL query that computes results dynamically on-the-fly when queried
Compresses table data
Encrypts sensitive customer records
quiz.explanation: A View is a stored virtual query. It occupies no physical data storage (unlike Materialized Views) and encapsulates complex joins, calculations, and security column filtering.

quiz.question: What is a Materialized View in databases like PostgreSQL and Oracle?
quiz.code: CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW monthly_summary AS ...
options: A view with graphics
A database view whose query results are physically computed and stored on disk, allowing fast querying of complex analytical aggregates with periodic REFRESH
A temporary view dropped upon session disconnect
A view editable by any user
quiz.explanation: Unlike standard virtual views, a Materialized View physically caches query results on disk. It provides lightning-fast reads on heavy aggregates and must be refreshed periodically.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of the 'LEAD()' and 'LAG()' window functions in SQL?
options: Measures query network latency
Accesses data from a subsequent (LEAD) or preceding (LAG) row at a specified physical offset without requiring a self-join
Sorts tables in reverse alphabetical order
Delays query execution
quiz.explanation: LAG() retrieves values from previous rows and LEAD() retrieves values from future rows within a window partition, making period-over-period delta calculations straightforward.

quiz.question: What is a Composite Key in relational database design?
options: An encrypted cryptographic key
A primary key or unique key composed of two or more combined columns to uniquely identify a record
A foreign key pointing to multiple databases
A generated UUID string
quiz.explanation: A Composite Key is a primary key that consists of two or more attributes combined (e.g. order_id + product_id in an order_items join table) to guarantee record uniqueness.

quiz.question: What is the role of the 'GROUP BY' clause in SQL?
quiz.code: SELECT department, COUNT(*), AVG(salary) FROM employees GROUP BY department;
options: Sorts rows in ascending alphabetical order
Collapses multiple rows with identical values in the specified columns into summary aggregate groups
Filters out rows with null values
Merges two tables into one
quiz.explanation: GROUP BY groups rows that have the same values in specified columns into summary rows, allowing aggregate functions (SUM, AVG, COUNT, MAX) to calculate values per group.

quiz.question: What rule must all columns in the SELECT clause follow when 'GROUP BY' is used?
options: All columns must be integers
Every column in the SELECT list must either be named in the GROUP BY clause or be enclosed within an aggregate function (e.g. SUM, MAX, COUNT)
Only one column is permitted in the SELECT list
GROUP BY columns cannot be aliased
quiz.explanation: Standard SQL requires every non-aggregated column in the SELECT statement to be explicitly listed in the GROUP BY clause to prevent non-deterministic multi-value projections.

quiz.question: What does the 'DISTINCT' keyword in a SELECT query do?
quiz.code: SELECT DISTINCT country FROM customers;
options: Sorts records alphabetically
Filters out duplicate rows from the query output, returning only unique values
Limits results to the first 10 rows
Selects only non-null values
quiz.explanation: DISTINCT evaluates the projected columns and eliminates duplicate rows, returning only unique combinations of values.

quiz.question: What does the 'BETWEEN low AND high' operator include in SQL?
quiz.code: SELECT * FROM products WHERE price BETWEEN 10 AND 50;
options: Values strictly greater than 10 and strictly less than 50 (exclusive)
Values greater than or equal to 10 and less than or equal to 50 (inclusive of both endpoints)
Only values that are multiples of 10
All values except those between 10 and 50
quiz.explanation: In standard SQL, the BETWEEN operator is inclusive: 'price BETWEEN 10 AND 50' is equivalent to 'price >= 10 AND price <= 50'.

quiz.question: What is a Database Transaction Savepoint ('SAVEPOINT')?
options: An automated backup of the database to disk
A marker within the scope of a transaction allowing selective partial rollback to that point without rolling back the entire transaction
A checkpoint where auto-commit is enabled
A constraint that prevents deletes
quiz.explanation: A SAVEPOINT establishes a named point within a transaction. Using 'ROLLBACK TO savepoint_name' undoes changes made after the savepoint while keeping earlier changes active.

quiz.question: What is a Database Deadlock?
options: A hard drive hardware crash
A situation where two or more transactions are blocked indefinitely, each waiting for locks held by the other in a circular dependency cycle
An expired user password
A query running longer than 10 seconds
quiz.explanation: A deadlock occurs when Transaction 1 holds Lock A and waits for Lock B, while Transaction 2 holds Lock B and waits for Lock A. Modern DBMSs detect deadlocks and abort one transaction.

quiz.question: What does the 'CASE' expression in SQL do?
quiz.code:
SELECT name,
  CASE 
    WHEN score >= 90 THEN 'A'
    WHEN score >= 80 THEN 'B'
    ELSE 'C'
  END AS grade
FROM students;
options: Converts lowercase characters to uppercase
Provides conditional if-then-else logic directly within SQL statements
Changes database table schemas
Executes stored procedures
quiz.explanation: The CASE expression is SQL's conditional expression, evaluating conditions sequentially and returning the matching THEN expression.

quiz.question: What does the 'OVER (PARTITION BY ...)' clause in SQL Window Functions do?
options: Partitions database tables across physical hard drives
Divides query result rows into separate groups (partitions) over which the window function calculates, without collapsing rows like GROUP BY does
Deletes duplicate rows in each partition
Sorts rows descending
quiz.explanation: PARTITION BY divides rows into groups to compute aggregate/ranking metrics per partition, but retains individual row identities without collapsing them into summary rows.

quiz.question: What is the result of 'SELECT 1 WHERE 1 = NULL;'?
options: Returns 1
Returns an empty result set (0 rows)
Returns NULL
Throws a syntax error
quiz.explanation: In SQL, comparing any value to NULL using '=' yields UNKNOWN. Since the WHERE clause only accepts expressions that evaluate to TRUE, the row is discarded.

quiz.question: What is an Index Seek versus an Index Scan in database execution plans?
options: They are identical operations
An Index Seek uses the B-Tree structure to navigate directly to specific matching keys in O(log n) time; an Index Scan traverses all or large sections of the index leaf pages in O(n) time
Index Scan is always faster than Index Seek
Index Seek requires no index
quiz.explanation: An Index Seek traverses the B-Tree index from root to leaf to locate matching rows directly. An Index Scan reads across leaf pages sequentially when queries lack high selectivity.

quiz.question: What is a Covering Index in SQL database optimization?
options: An index that covers the entire database

An index that contains all columns requested by a query (in keys or INCLUDE clause), allowing the query to be fulfilled entirely from the index without accessing the underlying table rows (eliminating Key/RID Lookups)
An index with a password
A primary key index only
quiz.explanation: A covering index contains all columns referenced in the SELECT, WHERE, and JOIN clauses. The query engine satisfies the request directly from the index B-tree without disk lookups to base tables.

quiz.question: What is a Database Trigger in SQL?
options: A tool to generate test mock data
A procedural code block automatically executed by the DBMS in response to specific DML events (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) on a specified table
An automated database backup cron
A query performance monitor
quiz.explanation: A trigger is a stored procedure automatically invoked by the database engine when DML modifications occur on a specified table, useful for audit logging and constraint enforcement.

quiz.question: What is the difference between a Stored Procedure and a User-Defined Function (UDF) in SQL?
options: UDFs can execute transactions while Stored Procedures cannot

Functions must return a value and cannot execute transaction control (COMMIT/ROLLBACK) or modify database state in SELECT queries; Stored Procedures do not require return values and can manage transactions and DML freely
Stored procedures cannot accept input parameters
Functions are compiled in C++ while procedures are Java
quiz.explanation: Functions must return values and are restricted to read-only computations in queries (no COMMIT/ROLLBACK). Stored Procedures perform business workflows, accept IN/OUT parameters, and manage transactions.

quiz.question: What does the SQL command 'ROLLBACK;' do?
options: Restores database backups from yesterday
Reverts all modifications performed in the current uncommitted transaction, restoring data to its state prior to the transaction's start
Deletes all database tables
Rolls the table schema back one version
quiz.explanation: ROLLBACK cancels all uncommitted data modifications performed in the active transaction, releasing all acquired locks and maintaining database consistency.

quiz.question: What is the function of the 'NTILE(4)' window function in SQL?
quiz.code: SELECT employee, salary, NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY salary) AS quartile FROM employees;
options: Multiplies salary by 4
Divides an ordered partition of rows into 4 as-equal-as-possible bucket groups (quartiles), numbering each row with its bucket number from 1 to 4
Selects the top 4 rows only
Filters out null salaries
quiz.explanation: NTILE(n) divides ordered rows into 'n' ranked buckets (e.g. NTILE(4) produces quartiles, NTILE(100) produces percentiles), assigning bucket numbers 1 through n.

quiz.question: What is a Candidate Key in relational database modeling?
options: A temporary key for testing
A minimal super key that contains no redundant attributes and can uniquely identify any record in the table (eligible to become the Primary Key)
A foreign key without an index
A column with numbers only
quiz.explanation: A Candidate Key is any column or minimal set of columns that uniquely identifies a row without redundant attributes. One candidate key is chosen as the Primary Key; the rest are alternate keys.

quiz.question: What does the 'EXCEPT' (or 'MINUS' in Oracle) set operator do?
quiz.code: SELECT user_id FROM signups EXCEPT SELECT user_id FROM active_subscriptions;
options: Combines both sets
Returns rows from the first query that DO NOT exist in the second query's result set
Throws an exception if duplicates exist
Returns only matching rows
quiz.explanation: EXCEPT (or MINUS) returns all distinct rows that appear in the first query result set but do not appear in the second query result set.

quiz.question: What is a Foreign Key constraint?
options: An encryption key from an external server
A column or combination of columns that establishes and enforces a link between data in two tables, ensuring referential integrity
A key that allows access from foreign IP addresses
A key generated by foreign databases
quiz.explanation: A Foreign Key establishes referential integrity by ensuring values in a child table column correspond to valid primary key values in a referenced parent table.

quiz.question: What does 'OPTIMIZE TABLE' or 'VACUUM' (in PostgreSQL) do?
options: Rewrites SQL queries to be shorter
Reclaims dead row storage left behind by UPDATE and DELETE operations, defragments pages, and updates optimizer table statistics
Deletes old database users
Restarts the database server
quiz.explanation: In MVCC architectures (like PostgreSQL), UPDATES create new row versions while DELETES mark rows dead. VACUUM reclaims dead tuple storage and updates table statistics for the query planner.

quiz.question: What is an SQL Injection attack and how is it reliably prevented?
options: A virus that crashes the SQL server; prevented by running antivirus
A vulnerability where malicious SQL commands are concatenated into dynamic queries; prevented by using Parameterized Queries (PreparedStatements) and ORMs
Overloading the database with too many queries; prevented with rate limits
A hardware power failure; prevented with UPS batteries
quiz.explanation: SQL Injection occurs when untrusted input is concatenated into query strings. Prepared Statements (parameterized queries) treat user inputs strictly as literal values rather than executable code.

SQL Multiple Choice Questions (MCQs) - 50 Practice Questions

Assessment ⏱️ 60 min 50 Questions

Test and master your SQL and Relational Database knowledge with this comprehensive set of 50 Multiple Choice Questions (MCQs) formatted in the classic GeeksforGeeks tutorial assessment style. Covering querying, joins, aggregations, subqueries, ACID properties, indexing, normalization, window functions, and transaction concurrency.

📝 Assessment Instructions

  • Each question has four potential choices: (A), (B), (C), and (D).
  • Review the problem statement and code snippet carefully before picking your answer.
  • Click on "💡 View Answer & Explanation" to reveal the correct option along with an in-depth technical explanation.

Question 1: What is the fundamental functional difference between the 'WHERE' clause and the 'HAVING' clause in SQL?

2 Points
A) No difference; they are completely interchangeable
B) 'WHERE' filters individual rows before grouping or aggregation; 'HAVING' filters aggregated group records after the 'GROUP BY' clause has been processed ✓ Correct
C) 'HAVING' can only be used with subqueries
D) 'WHERE' is only used for numerical values
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) 'WHERE' filters individual rows before grouping or aggregation; 'HAVING' filters aggregated group records after the 'GROUP BY' clause has been processed

Explanation: 'WHERE' filters individual rows before aggregation functions are evaluated. 'HAVING' filters aggregated rows created by the 'GROUP BY' clause (e.g. HAVING COUNT(*) > 5).

Question 2: Which JOIN type returns all records from the left table and matching records from the right table, populating NULL for non-matching right table columns?

2 Points
A) INNER JOIN
B) LEFT JOIN (LEFT OUTER JOIN) ✓ Correct
C) FULL OUTER JOIN
D) CROSS JOIN
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) LEFT JOIN (LEFT OUTER JOIN)

Explanation: A LEFT JOIN preserves every row from the left-hand table. If no corresponding match exists in the right-hand table, all right-hand column values in that row will be NULL.

Question 3: What does the 'A' in ACID properties of relational database transactions guarantee?

2 Points
A) Asynchronous execution
B) Atomicity: guarantees that all operations within a transaction complete successfully or the entire transaction is rolled back with zero changes applied (all-or-nothing) ✓ Correct
C) Authentication
D) Association
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) Atomicity: guarantees that all operations within a transaction complete successfully or the entire transaction is rolled back with zero changes applied (all-or-nothing)

Explanation: Atomicity ensures that transactions are treated as single indivisible units of work: either all database statements succeed or, upon failure, the entire transaction is rolled back.

Question 4: What is the key operational difference between 'TRUNCATE' and 'DELETE' statements in SQL?

2 Points
A) DELETE cannot be rolled back; TRUNCATE can always be rolled back
B) DELETE is a DML command that removes rows one by one, writes row deletions to the transaction log, supports WHERE clauses, and fires triggers; TRUNCATE is a DDL command that deallocates entire data pages, is faster, and cannot have a WHERE clause ✓ Correct
C) TRUNCATE deletes the table schema definition itself
D) There is no difference
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) DELETE is a DML command that removes rows one by one, writes row deletions to the transaction log, supports WHERE clauses, and fires triggers; TRUNCATE is a DDL command that deallocates entire data pages, is faster, and cannot have a WHERE clause

Explanation: DELETE (DML) logs row deletions individually and fires triggers, allowing row-level WHERE filtering. TRUNCATE (DDL) deallocates data pages directly, resets identity counters, and operates significantly faster.

Question 5: What data structure is most universally utilized for relational database indexes to support fast lookups and range scans?

2 Points
A) Binary Heap
B) B-Tree / B+Tree ✓ Correct
C) Hash Table only
D) Linked List
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) B-Tree / B+Tree

Explanation: B+Trees maintain sorted keys with balanced depth. Leaf nodes are linked sequentially, allowing both O(log n) random key lookups and highly efficient range-based scans.

Question 6: What is the difference between 'UNION' and 'UNION ALL' when combining the results of two SELECT queries?

2 Points
A) UNION ALL removes duplicate records; UNION keeps all duplicates
B) UNION performs a distinct sort operation to eliminate duplicate rows from the final result; UNION ALL combines all rows from both sets without removing duplicates, making it faster ✓ Correct
C) UNION only works with numbers
D) UNION ALL requires identical table names
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) UNION performs a distinct sort operation to eliminate duplicate rows from the final result; UNION ALL combines all rows from both sets without removing duplicates, making it faster

Explanation: UNION deduplicates the combined dataset (incurring a sort/hash overhead). UNION ALL simply concatenates result sets without deduplication, offering superior query performance.

Question 7: What is the difference between 'COUNT(*)' and 'COUNT(column_name)'?

2 Points
A) No difference
B) 'COUNT(*)' counts all rows in the group including rows with NULL values; 'COUNT(column_name)' counts only rows where the specified column is NOT NULL ✓ Correct
C) 'COUNT(*)' is slower than 'COUNT(column)'
D) 'COUNT(column)' returns 0 if any row is null
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) 'COUNT(*)' counts all rows in the group including rows with NULL values; 'COUNT(column_name)' counts only rows where the specified column is NOT NULL

Explanation: COUNT(*) tallies all rows returned by the query regardless of contents. COUNT(column_name) evaluates and excludes NULL values from the total count.

Question 8: Which SQL constraint ensures that all values in a column are unique and automatically prevents NULL values?

2 Points
A) UNIQUE
B) PRIMARY KEY ✓ Correct
C) FOREIGN KEY
D) CHECK
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) PRIMARY KEY

Explanation: A PRIMARY KEY uniquely identifies each record in a table. It implicitly combines UNIQUE and NOT NULL constraints. Standard UNIQUE constraints typically allow one or more NULL values.

Question 9: What does the 'ON DELETE CASCADE' clause on a Foreign Key constraint enforce?

2 Points 
CONSTRAINT fk_user FOREIGN KEY (user_id) REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE
A) Prevents the parent record from being deleted
B) Automatically deletes all associated child rows in this table whenever the corresponding referenced parent row is deleted ✓ Correct
C) Sets the foreign key column to NULL upon parent deletion
D) Archives deleted rows into a backup table
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) Automatically deletes all associated child rows in this table whenever the corresponding referenced parent row is deleted

Explanation: 'ON DELETE CASCADE' automatically propagates parent row deletions to dependent child rows, preventing orphaned records and foreign key constraint violations.

Question 10: What is the difference between 'RANK()' and 'DENSE_RANK()' window functions when ranking ties?

2 Points
A) No difference
B) 'RANK()' assigns identical ranks to ties but skips subsequent rank numbers (e.g. 1, 2, 2, 4); 'DENSE_RANK()' assigns identical ranks to ties without skipping subsequent numbers (e.g. 1, 2, 2, 3) ✓ Correct
C) 'DENSE_RANK()' only ranks descending order
D) 'RANK()' returns floating point values
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) 'RANK()' assigns identical ranks to ties but skips subsequent rank numbers (e.g. 1, 2, 2, 4); 'DENSE_RANK()' assigns identical ranks to ties without skipping subsequent numbers (e.g. 1, 2, 2, 3)

Explanation: When ties occur: RANK() introduces gaps in the ranking sequence (1, 2, 2, 4). DENSE_RANK() leaves no gaps (1, 2, 2, 3). ROW_NUMBER() always assigns strict sequential integers (1, 2, 3, 4).

Question 11: What does the 'COALESCE(val1, val2, val3)' function return?

2 Points 
SELECT COALESCE(phone, mobile, 'N/A') FROM contacts;
A) Concatenates all non-null values together
B) Returns the first non-null expression from the argument list, or NULL if all arguments evaluate to NULL ✓ Correct
C) Counts the number of null values
D) Returns the maximum value
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) Returns the first non-null expression from the argument list, or NULL if all arguments evaluate to NULL

Explanation: COALESCE() evaluates its arguments sequentially from left to right and returns the first non-NULL expression, providing a clean fallback mechanism.

Question 12: In an SQL LIKE pattern, what do the '%' and '_' wildcard characters represent?

2 Points 
SELECT * FROM users WHERE name LIKE 'J_n%';
A) '%' matches exactly one character; '_' matches zero or more characters
B) '%' matches zero, one, or multiple characters; '_' matches exactly one single character ✓ Correct
C) Both characters match any single digit
D) '%' matches numbers; '_' matches letters
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) '%' matches zero, one, or multiple characters; '_' matches exactly one single character

Explanation: In SQL LIKE clauses: '%' matches any sequence of zero or more characters. '_' matches exactly one single character (e.g. 'J_n%' matches 'Jane', 'Jonny', 'Junior').

Question 13: What is a Correlated Subquery in SQL?

2 Points
A) A subquery that runs once before the outer query starts
B) A subquery that references columns from the enclosing outer query and is evaluated once for each candidate row processed by the outer query ✓ Correct
C) A subquery that joins two databases
D) A subquery containing a UNION
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) A subquery that references columns from the enclosing outer query and is evaluated once for each candidate row processed by the outer query

Explanation: A correlated subquery references columns from the outer query. Because it depends on outer row data, it re-evaluates repeatedly for every row considered by the outer query.

Question 14: What is the difference between 'EXISTS' and 'IN' when evaluating subqueries?

2 Points
A) No difference
B) 'EXISTS' tests for the existence of rows and short-circuits to TRUE as soon as a single match is located; 'IN' scans and evaluates the entire subquery result set and handles NULLs differently ✓ Correct
C) 'IN' is always faster than 'EXISTS'
D) 'EXISTS' cannot be used with WHERE
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) 'EXISTS' tests for the existence of rows and short-circuits to TRUE as soon as a single match is located; 'IN' scans and evaluates the entire subquery result set and handles NULLs differently

Explanation: EXISTS returns a boolean as soon as the first matching row is found (short-circuit). IN compiles an in-memory list and can yield unexpected results if NULL values are present (NOT IN with NULL returns empty).

Question 15: What is Database Normalization and what is its primary objective?

2 Points
A) To increase the speed of SELECT queries by duplicating data across tables
B) To organize database schemas to eliminate redundant data and prevent insertion, update, and deletion anomalies ✓ Correct
C) To convert SQL tables into JSON files
D) To compress disk storage using gzip
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) To organize database schemas to eliminate redundant data and prevent insertion, update, and deletion anomalies

Explanation: Normalization organizes relational tables to ensure dependencies make sense (1NF, 2NF, 3NF), minimizing duplicate data to prevent data inconsistency and modification anomalies.

Question 16: What requirement must a table satisfy to be in Third Normal Form (3NF)?

2 Points
A) It must be in 2NF and have no partial key dependencies
B) It must be in 2NF and contain NO transitive dependencies (no non-key attribute can depend on another non-key attribute) ✓ Correct
C) It must have no foreign keys
D) All columns must be strings
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) It must be in 2NF and contain NO transitive dependencies (no non-key attribute can depend on another non-key attribute)

Explanation: 3NF requires a relation to be in 2NF and have every non-prime attribute non-transitively dependent on the primary key (X -> Y requires X to be a super key or Y to be a prime attribute).

Question 17: What is the difference between a Clustered Index and a Non-Clustered Index?

2 Points
A) A table can have multiple clustered indexes but only one non-clustered index
B) A Clustered Index dictates the physical order in which actual table rows are stored on disk (only one per table, usually the Primary Key); a Non-Clustered Index stores sorted keys with pointers back to the data rows ✓ Correct
C) Non-clustered indexes are stored in RAM only
D) Clustered indexes are slower for range scans
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) A Clustered Index dictates the physical order in which actual table rows are stored on disk (only one per table, usually the Primary Key); a Non-Clustered Index stores sorted keys with pointers back to the data rows

Explanation: A clustered index physically sorts and stores data rows on disk (hence max 1 per table). Non-clustered indexes are separate auxiliary B-Trees containing indexed columns and row locators/pointers.

Question 18: What is a Common Table Expression (CTE) in SQL?

2 Points 
WITH RegionalSales AS (
  SELECT region, SUM(amount) AS total FROM sales GROUP BY region
)
SELECT * FROM RegionalSales WHERE total > 100000;
A) A temporary physical table saved to disk
B) A named temporary result set defined within the execution scope of a single SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE statement using the 'WITH' clause ✓ Correct
C) A database trigger
D) An encrypted view
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) A named temporary result set defined within the execution scope of a single SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE statement using the 'WITH' clause

Explanation: A CTE (Common Table Expression) created with 'WITH name AS (...)' provides a readable, modular, and optionally recursive temporary query block that exists only during query execution.

Question 19: What does a CROSS JOIN produce?

2 Points 
SELECT * FROM colors CROSS JOIN sizes;
A) Only matching rows between both tables
B) The Cartesian Product: every row from the first table paired with every row from the second table (M * N rows) ✓ Correct
C) An empty table
D) A full outer join without nulls
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) The Cartesian Product: every row from the first table paired with every row from the second table (M * N rows)

Explanation: A CROSS JOIN produces the Cartesian product of the two tables. If table A has 5 rows and table B has 10 rows, the result contains 50 rows.

Question 20: What is a SELF JOIN?

2 Points 
SELECT e.name, m.name AS manager 
FROM employees e 
JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id;
A) A query that joins a table to itself using table aliases to represent parent-child or hierarchical relationships ✓ Correct
B) A join between two databases on the same host
C) An automatic query without an ON clause
D) A circular dependency error
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (A) A query that joins a table to itself using table aliases to represent parent-child or hierarchical relationships

Explanation: A self-join joins a table to itself using distinct aliases (e.g. employee 'e' and manager 'm'), commonly used to model hierarchies, organizational charts, or sequential events.

Question 21: Which transaction isolation level provides the highest degree of isolation and completely prevents Dirty Reads, Non-Repeatable Reads, and Phantom Reads?

2 Points
A) READ UNCOMMITTED
B) READ COMMITTED
C) REPEATABLE READ
D) SERIALIZABLE ✓ Correct
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (D) SERIALIZABLE

Explanation: SERIALIZABLE is the strictest ACID isolation level. It executes concurrent transactions as if they were processed sequentially one after another, eliminating dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and phantom reads.

Question 22: What is a 'Dirty Read' in database transaction concurrency?

2 Points
A) Reading corrupt disk sectors
B) A transaction reads uncommitted changes made by another concurrently running transaction that might subsequently be rolled back ✓ Correct
C) Reading data without an index
D) Reading deleted foreign keys
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) A transaction reads uncommitted changes made by another concurrently running transaction that might subsequently be rolled back

Explanation: A dirty read occurs when Transaction A reads data modified by Transaction B before Transaction B commits. If B rolls back, Transaction A operated on invalid, phantom data.

Question 23: What is the difference between a 'Non-Repeatable Read' and a 'Phantom Read'?

2 Points
A) No difference
B) Non-Repeatable Read occurs when re-reading the SAME row yields modified column data; Phantom Read occurs when re-executing a range query yields NEWLY INSERTED or deleted rows matching the search criteria ✓ Correct
C) Phantom reads only happen in MySQL
D) Non-repeatable reads happen during database backup
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) Non-Repeatable Read occurs when re-reading the SAME row yields modified column data; Phantom Read occurs when re-executing a range query yields NEWLY INSERTED or deleted rows matching the search criteria

Explanation: Non-repeatable read: an existing row's values change between reads due to an UPDATE. Phantom read: the set of rows satisfying a query range predicate changes due to concurrent INSERT/DELETE.

Question 24: What is the function of the 'EXPLAIN' or 'EXPLAIN ANALYZE' command in SQL?

2 Points 
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 450;
A) Translates SQL to English sentences
B) Displays the Query Execution Plan generated by the database optimizer, detailing index scans, sequential scans, join algorithms, estimated costs, and actual runtime execution timings ✓ Correct
C) Checks for SQL syntax errors without running
D) Repairs corrupted table indexes
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) Displays the Query Execution Plan generated by the database optimizer, detailing index scans, sequential scans, join algorithms, estimated costs, and actual runtime execution timings

Explanation: EXPLAIN displays the database optimizer's planned execution steps (Index Scan vs Seq Scan, Hash Join vs Nested Loop, buffer usage, and execution timings), essential for query optimization.

Question 25: What does the 'NULLIF(a, b)' function return?

2 Points 
SELECT 100 / NULLIF(divisor, 0) FROM calculations;
A) Returns a if a is null
B) Returns NULL if both arguments are equal (a == b); otherwise returns the first argument 'a' ✓ Correct
C) Throws an error if either argument is null
D) Returns 0
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) Returns NULL if both arguments are equal (a == b); otherwise returns the first argument 'a'

Explanation: NULLIF(a, b) returns NULL if a = b; otherwise it returns a. It is universally employed to prevent division-by-zero errors (NULLIF(divisor, 0) turns 0 into NULL, yielding NULL instead of crashing).

Question 26: What happens when you compare a column to NULL using '= NULL' instead of 'IS NULL'?

2 Points 
SELECT * FROM users WHERE status = NULL;
A) Returns all rows where status is NULL
B) Returns an empty result set (0 rows) because in SQL, comparison with NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN (Three-Valued Logic), never TRUE ✓ Correct
C) Throws a compile-time syntax error
D) Returns all non-null rows
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) Returns an empty result set (0 rows) because in SQL, comparison with NULL evaluates to UNKNOWN (Three-Valued Logic), never TRUE

Explanation: In SQL's Three-Valued Logic (TRUE, FALSE, UNKNOWN), any equality comparison with NULL (e.g. col = NULL) yields UNKNOWN. Since WHERE requires TRUE, zero rows are returned. You must use 'IS NULL'.

Question 27: What is the purpose of a Database View ('CREATE VIEW')?

2 Points 
CREATE VIEW active_customers AS 
SELECT id, name, email FROM customers WHERE active = true;
A) Creates an identical physical copy of the table on disk
B) Creates a virtual table defined by an underlying stored SQL query that computes results dynamically on-the-fly when queried ✓ Correct
C) Compresses table data
D) Encrypts sensitive customer records
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) Creates a virtual table defined by an underlying stored SQL query that computes results dynamically on-the-fly when queried

Explanation: A View is a stored virtual query. It occupies no physical data storage (unlike Materialized Views) and encapsulates complex joins, calculations, and security column filtering.

Question 28: What is a Materialized View in databases like PostgreSQL and Oracle?

2 Points 
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW monthly_summary AS ...
A) A view with graphics
B) A database view whose query results are physically computed and stored on disk, allowing fast querying of complex analytical aggregates with periodic REFRESH ✓ Correct
C) A temporary view dropped upon session disconnect
D) A view editable by any user
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) A database view whose query results are physically computed and stored on disk, allowing fast querying of complex analytical aggregates with periodic REFRESH

Explanation: Unlike standard virtual views, a Materialized View physically caches query results on disk. It provides lightning-fast reads on heavy aggregates and must be refreshed periodically.

Question 29: What is the purpose of the 'LEAD()' and 'LAG()' window functions in SQL?

2 Points 
SELECT date, revenue,
       LAG(revenue, 1) OVER (ORDER BY date) AS previous_day_revenue
FROM daily_sales;
A) Measures query network latency
B) Accesses data from a subsequent (LEAD) or preceding (LAG) row at a specified physical offset without requiring a self-join ✓ Correct
C) Sorts tables in reverse alphabetical order
D) Delays query execution
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) Accesses data from a subsequent (LEAD) or preceding (LAG) row at a specified physical offset without requiring a self-join

Explanation: LAG() retrieves values from previous rows and LEAD() retrieves values from future rows within a window partition, making period-over-period delta calculations straightforward.

Question 30: What is a Composite Key in relational database design?

2 Points
A) An encrypted cryptographic key
B) A primary key or unique key composed of two or more combined columns to uniquely identify a record ✓ Correct
C) A foreign key pointing to multiple databases
D) A generated UUID string
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) A primary key or unique key composed of two or more combined columns to uniquely identify a record

Explanation: A Composite Key is a primary key that consists of two or more attributes combined (e.g. order_id + product_id in an order_items join table) to guarantee record uniqueness.

Question 31: What is the role of the 'GROUP BY' clause in SQL?

2 Points 
SELECT department, COUNT(*), AVG(salary) FROM employees GROUP BY department;
A) Sorts rows in ascending alphabetical order
B) Collapses multiple rows with identical values in the specified columns into summary aggregate groups ✓ Correct
C) Filters out rows with null values
D) Merges two tables into one
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) Collapses multiple rows with identical values in the specified columns into summary aggregate groups

Explanation: GROUP BY groups rows that have the same values in specified columns into summary rows, allowing aggregate functions (SUM, AVG, COUNT, MAX) to calculate values per group.

Question 32: What rule must all columns in the SELECT clause follow when 'GROUP BY' is used?

2 Points
A) All columns must be integers
B) Every column in the SELECT list must either be named in the GROUP BY clause or be enclosed within an aggregate function (e.g. SUM, MAX, COUNT) ✓ Correct
C) Only one column is permitted in the SELECT list
D) GROUP BY columns cannot be aliased
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) Every column in the SELECT list must either be named in the GROUP BY clause or be enclosed within an aggregate function (e.g. SUM, MAX, COUNT)

Explanation: Standard SQL requires every non-aggregated column in the SELECT statement to be explicitly listed in the GROUP BY clause to prevent non-deterministic multi-value projections.

Question 33: What does the 'DISTINCT' keyword in a SELECT query do?

2 Points 
SELECT DISTINCT country FROM customers;
A) Sorts records alphabetically
B) Filters out duplicate rows from the query output, returning only unique values ✓ Correct
C) Limits results to the first 10 rows
D) Selects only non-null values
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) Filters out duplicate rows from the query output, returning only unique values

Explanation: DISTINCT evaluates the projected columns and eliminates duplicate rows, returning only unique combinations of values.

Question 34: What does the 'BETWEEN low AND high' operator include in SQL?

2 Points 
SELECT * FROM products WHERE price BETWEEN 10 AND 50;
A) Values strictly greater than 10 and strictly less than 50 (exclusive)
B) Values greater than or equal to 10 and less than or equal to 50 (inclusive of both endpoints) ✓ Correct
C) Only values that are multiples of 10
D) All values except those between 10 and 50
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) Values greater than or equal to 10 and less than or equal to 50 (inclusive of both endpoints)

Explanation: In standard SQL, the BETWEEN operator is inclusive: 'price BETWEEN 10 AND 50' is equivalent to 'price >= 10 AND price <= 50'.

Question 35: What is a Database Transaction Savepoint ('SAVEPOINT')?

2 Points 
SAVEPOINT sp1;
-- operations
ROLLBACK TO sp1;
A) An automated backup of the database to disk
B) A marker within the scope of a transaction allowing selective partial rollback to that point without rolling back the entire transaction ✓ Correct
C) A checkpoint where auto-commit is enabled
D) A constraint that prevents deletes
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) A marker within the scope of a transaction allowing selective partial rollback to that point without rolling back the entire transaction

Explanation: A SAVEPOINT establishes a named point within a transaction. Using 'ROLLBACK TO savepoint_name' undoes changes made after the savepoint while keeping earlier changes active.

Question 36: What is a Database Deadlock?

2 Points
A) A hard drive hardware crash
B) A situation where two or more transactions are blocked indefinitely, each waiting for locks held by the other in a circular dependency cycle ✓ Correct
C) An expired user password
D) A query running longer than 10 seconds
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) A situation where two or more transactions are blocked indefinitely, each waiting for locks held by the other in a circular dependency cycle

Explanation: A deadlock occurs when Transaction 1 holds Lock A and waits for Lock B, while Transaction 2 holds Lock B and waits for Lock A. Modern DBMSs detect deadlocks and abort one transaction.

Question 37: What does the 'CASE' expression in SQL do?

2 Points 
SELECT name,
  CASE 
    WHEN score >= 90 THEN 'A'
    WHEN score >= 80 THEN 'B'
    ELSE 'C'
  END AS grade
FROM students;
A) Converts lowercase characters to uppercase
B) Provides conditional if-then-else logic directly within SQL statements ✓ Correct
C) Changes database table schemas
D) Executes stored procedures
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) Provides conditional if-then-else logic directly within SQL statements

Explanation: The CASE expression is SQL's conditional expression, evaluating conditions sequentially and returning the matching THEN expression.

Question 38: What does the 'OVER (PARTITION BY ...)' clause in SQL Window Functions do?

2 Points 
SELECT employee, department, salary,
       AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department) AS dept_avg
FROM employees;
A) Partitions database tables across physical hard drives
B) Divides query result rows into separate groups (partitions) over which the window function calculates, without collapsing rows like GROUP BY does ✓ Correct
C) Deletes duplicate rows in each partition
D) Sorts rows descending
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) Divides query result rows into separate groups (partitions) over which the window function calculates, without collapsing rows like GROUP BY does

Explanation: PARTITION BY divides rows into groups to compute aggregate/ranking metrics per partition, but retains individual row identities without collapsing them into summary rows.

Question 39: What is the result of 'SELECT 1 WHERE 1 = NULL;'?

2 Points
A) Returns 1
B) Returns an empty result set (0 rows) ✓ Correct
C) Returns NULL
D) Throws a syntax error
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) Returns an empty result set (0 rows)

Explanation: In SQL, comparing any value to NULL using '=' yields UNKNOWN. Since the WHERE clause only accepts expressions that evaluate to TRUE, the row is discarded.

Question 40: What is an Index Seek versus an Index Scan in database execution plans?

2 Points
A) They are identical operations
B) An Index Seek uses the B-Tree structure to navigate directly to specific matching keys in O(log n) time; an Index Scan traverses all or large sections of the index leaf pages in O(n) time ✓ Correct
C) Index Scan is always faster than Index Seek
D) Index Seek requires no index
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) An Index Seek uses the B-Tree structure to navigate directly to specific matching keys in O(log n) time; an Index Scan traverses all or large sections of the index leaf pages in O(n) time

Explanation: An Index Seek traverses the B-Tree index from root to leaf to locate matching rows directly. An Index Scan reads across leaf pages sequentially when queries lack high selectivity.

Question 41: What is a Covering Index in SQL database optimization?

2 Points
A) An index that covers the entire database
B) An index that contains all columns requested by a query (in keys or INCLUDE clause), allowing the query to be fulfilled entirely from the index without accessing the underlying table rows (eliminating Key/RID Lookups) ✓ Correct
C) An index with a password
D) A primary key index only
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) An index that contains all columns requested by a query (in keys or INCLUDE clause), allowing the query to be fulfilled entirely from the index without accessing the underlying table rows (eliminating Key/RID Lookups)

Explanation: A covering index contains all columns referenced in the SELECT, WHERE, and JOIN clauses. The query engine satisfies the request directly from the index B-tree without disk lookups to base tables.

Question 42: What is a Database Trigger in SQL?

2 Points 
CREATE TRIGGER update_timestamp 
BEFORE UPDATE ON accounts 
FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE PROCEDURE set_timestamp();
A) A tool to generate test mock data
B) A procedural code block automatically executed by the DBMS in response to specific DML events (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) on a specified table ✓ Correct
C) An automated database backup cron
D) A query performance monitor
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) A procedural code block automatically executed by the DBMS in response to specific DML events (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) on a specified table

Explanation: A trigger is a stored procedure automatically invoked by the database engine when DML modifications occur on a specified table, useful for audit logging and constraint enforcement.

Question 43: What is the difference between a Stored Procedure and a User-Defined Function (UDF) in SQL?

2 Points
A) UDFs can execute transactions while Stored Procedures cannot
B) Functions must return a value and cannot execute transaction control (COMMIT/ROLLBACK) or modify database state in SELECT queries; Stored Procedures do not require return values and can manage transactions and DML freely ✓ Correct
C) Stored procedures cannot accept input parameters
D) Functions are compiled in C++ while procedures are Java
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) Functions must return a value and cannot execute transaction control (COMMIT/ROLLBACK) or modify database state in SELECT queries; Stored Procedures do not require return values and can manage transactions and DML freely

Explanation: Functions must return values and are restricted to read-only computations in queries (no COMMIT/ROLLBACK). Stored Procedures perform business workflows, accept IN/OUT parameters, and manage transactions.

Question 44: What does the SQL command 'ROLLBACK;' do?

2 Points
A) Restores database backups from yesterday
B) Reverts all modifications performed in the current uncommitted transaction, restoring data to its state prior to the transaction's start ✓ Correct
C) Deletes all database tables
D) Rolls the table schema back one version
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) Reverts all modifications performed in the current uncommitted transaction, restoring data to its state prior to the transaction's start

Explanation: ROLLBACK cancels all uncommitted data modifications performed in the active transaction, releasing all acquired locks and maintaining database consistency.

Question 45: What is the function of the 'NTILE(4)' window function in SQL?

2 Points 
SELECT employee, salary, NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY salary) AS quartile FROM employees;
A) Multiplies salary by 4
B) Divides an ordered partition of rows into 4 as-equal-as-possible bucket groups (quartiles), numbering each row with its bucket number from 1 to 4 ✓ Correct
C) Selects the top 4 rows only
D) Filters out null salaries
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) Divides an ordered partition of rows into 4 as-equal-as-possible bucket groups (quartiles), numbering each row with its bucket number from 1 to 4

Explanation: NTILE(n) divides ordered rows into 'n' ranked buckets (e.g. NTILE(4) produces quartiles, NTILE(100) produces percentiles), assigning bucket numbers 1 through n.

Question 46: What is a Candidate Key in relational database modeling?

2 Points
A) A temporary key for testing
B) A minimal super key that contains no redundant attributes and can uniquely identify any record in the table (eligible to become the Primary Key) ✓ Correct
C) A foreign key without an index
D) A column with numbers only
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) A minimal super key that contains no redundant attributes and can uniquely identify any record in the table (eligible to become the Primary Key)

Explanation: A Candidate Key is any column or minimal set of columns that uniquely identifies a row without redundant attributes. One candidate key is chosen as the Primary Key; the rest are alternate keys.

Question 47: What does the 'EXCEPT' (or 'MINUS' in Oracle) set operator do?

2 Points 
SELECT user_id FROM signups EXCEPT SELECT user_id FROM active_subscriptions;
A) Combines both sets
B) Returns rows from the first query that DO NOT exist in the second query's result set ✓ Correct
C) Throws an exception if duplicates exist
D) Returns only matching rows
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) Returns rows from the first query that DO NOT exist in the second query's result set

Explanation: EXCEPT (or MINUS) returns all distinct rows that appear in the first query result set but do not appear in the second query result set.

Question 48: What is a Foreign Key constraint?

2 Points
A) An encryption key from an external server
B) A column or combination of columns that establishes and enforces a link between data in two tables, ensuring referential integrity ✓ Correct
C) A key that allows access from foreign IP addresses
D) A key generated by foreign databases
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) A column or combination of columns that establishes and enforces a link between data in two tables, ensuring referential integrity

Explanation: A Foreign Key establishes referential integrity by ensuring values in a child table column correspond to valid primary key values in a referenced parent table.

Question 49: What does 'OPTIMIZE TABLE' or 'VACUUM' (in PostgreSQL) do?

2 Points
A) Rewrites SQL queries to be shorter
B) Reclaims dead row storage left behind by UPDATE and DELETE operations, defragments pages, and updates optimizer table statistics ✓ Correct
C) Deletes old database users
D) Restarts the database server
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) Reclaims dead row storage left behind by UPDATE and DELETE operations, defragments pages, and updates optimizer table statistics

Explanation: In MVCC architectures (like PostgreSQL), UPDATES create new row versions while DELETES mark rows dead. VACUUM reclaims dead tuple storage and updates table statistics for the query planner.

Question 50: What is an SQL Injection attack and how is it reliably prevented?

2 Points
A) A virus that crashes the SQL server; prevented by running antivirus
B) A vulnerability where malicious SQL commands are concatenated into dynamic queries; prevented by using Parameterized Queries (PreparedStatements) and ORMs ✓ Correct
C) Overloading the database with too many queries; prevented with rate limits
D) A hardware power failure; prevented with UPS batteries
💡 View Answer & Explanation

Answer: (B) A vulnerability where malicious SQL commands are concatenated into dynamic queries; prevented by using Parameterized Queries (PreparedStatements) and ORMs

Explanation: SQL Injection occurs when untrusted input is concatenated into query strings. Prepared Statements (parameterized queries) treat user inputs strictly as literal values rather than executable code.

SQL Interview Questions & Answers

Interview Preparation ⏱️ 20 min read

Curated technical interview questions covering foundational principles, edge cases, and high-level architectural patterns frequently encountered in SQL developer interviews.

Q1: Explain ACID Properties in Relational Databases.

Easy
📖 View Technical Answer & Deep-Dive
ACID guarantees reliable processing of database transactions:
  • Atomicity: All-or-nothing. If any operation within the transaction fails, the entire transaction is rolled back.
  • Consistency: Ensures transactions transition the database from one valid state to another, maintaining all constraints and triggers.
  • Isolation: Concurrent transactions execute independently without interfering with each other (preventing dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, or phantom reads).
  • Durability: Once a transaction is committed, changes survive system failures or crashes (persisted to disk via write-ahead logging).

Q2: Explain Database Normalization and the stages 1NF, 2NF, and 3NF.

Medium
📖 View Technical Answer & Deep-Dive
Normalization organizes table structures to minimize data redundancy and prevent insertion, update, and deletion anomalies:
  • 1NF (First Normal Form): Each column contains atomic (indivisible) values, and each record is unique (Primary Key exists).
  • 2NF (Second Normal Form): In 1NF AND no non-key attribute is partially dependent on any candidate key (eliminates partial functional dependencies in composite keys).
  • 3NF (Third Normal Form): In 2NF AND no non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute (eliminates transitive functional dependencies).

Q3: What is the difference between ROW_NUMBER(), RANK(), and DENSE_RANK() in SQL Window Functions?

Medium
📖 View Technical Answer & Deep-Dive
When ordering data with ties (identical values):
  • ROW_NUMBER(): Assigns a strict sequential integer (1, 2, 3, 4) with zero duplicates regardless of ties.
  • RANK(): Assigns identical rank to ties, but skips subsequent rank numbers (e.g. 1, 2, 2, 4).
  • DENSE_RANK(): Assigns identical rank to ties, but does NOT skip any rank numbers (e.g. 1, 2, 2, 3).

Q4: How do Database Indexes work and when do they negatively impact performance?

Hard
📖 View Technical Answer & Deep-Dive
A database index (typically a B+Tree) is a specialized auxiliary data structure that holds sorted key values alongside pointers to actual table row locations on disk.

Performance Trade-offs:
  • Positive: Accelerates SELECT queries with WHERE filters, ORDER BY sorts, and JOIN conditions from O(N) full table scans down to O(log N).
  • Negative: Degrades write operations (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) because every index must be modified and rebalanced. Excessive indexing also consumes significant RAM and storage.
